subject: Biology
title: The Water Cycle
description: A quick, practical guide to The Water Cycle.

hook.text: The water you drank today may have once been drunk by a dinosaur. Water recycles endlessly.

buildup.text: The sun evaporates water from oceans. It rises, cools, condenses into clouds, and falls as rain.

discovery.text: Plants pull water from soil and release it as vapor through transpiration—a hidden pump.

twist.text: The Amazon rainforest generates half its own rainfall by recycling water through transpiration.

climax.text: Deforestation disrupts local water cycles, reducing rainfall and drying out entire regions.

punchline.text: Every drop of water has a story billions of years old.

quiz.question: How does the Amazon rainforest generate much of its own rainfall?

details.summary: The water cycle circulates water between the atmosphere, land, and oceans through evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and runoff. Solar energy drives evaporation from surfaces, plants release water through transpiration, and gravity returns water to oceans via rivers and groundwater.
details.whyItMatters: The water cycle distributes freshwater essential for all life and shapes landscapes through erosion and deposition. Climate change is intensifying the cycle, producing more extreme droughts and floods in different regions.
takeaways: About 97 percent of Earth's water is saltwater in the oceans
Plants return significant water to the atmosphere through transpiration
Climate change intensifies the water cycle making droughts and floods worse

faq.question: How much of Earth's water is available as freshwater?
faq.answer: About 97 percent is saltwater. Of the 3 percent that is freshwater, most is locked in ice caps and glaciers. Less than 1 percent of all water on Earth is accessible freshwater in rivers, lakes, and shallow groundwater available for human use.

faq.question: How does climate change affect the water cycle?
faq.answer: Warmer air holds more moisture, intensifying evaporation and precipitation. Wet regions tend to get wetter while dry regions get drier. Glaciers and snowpack that millions depend on for summer water are shrinking, altering river flows and water availability.
